'''''Pistia''''' is a genus of [[aquatic plant]]s in the [[arum]] family, [[Araceae]]. It is the sole genus in the tribe '''''Pistieae''''' which reflects its systematic isolation within the family.<ref name=":4">{{cite journal |last1=Buzgo |first1=Matyas |title=Inflorescence development of Pistia stratiotes (Araceae) |journal=Botanische Jahrbücher für Systematik, Pflanzengeschichte und Pflanzengeographie |date=1994 |volume=115 |issue=1 |page=557 |doi=10.1186/1999-3110-55-30|pmid=28510972 |pmc=5432749 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The single species it comprises, '''''Pistia stratiotes''''', is often called '''water cabbage''', '''water lettuce''', '''Nile cabbage''', or '''shellflower'''. Its native distribution is uncertain but is probably [[pantropical]]; it was first scientifically described from plants found on the [[Nile]] near [[Lake Victoria]] in [[Africa]].<ref name="Indian Medicinal" /> It is now present, either naturally or through human introduction, in nearly all tropical and subtropical fresh waterways and is considered an [[invasive species]] as well as a mosquito breeding habitat. The specific epithet is derived from a Greek word, στρατιώτης, meaning "soldier", which references the sword-shaped leaves of some plants in the genus ''[[Stratiotes]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=stratiotes|url=http://plantillustrations.org/epithet.php?id_epithet=201508&mobile=1&uhd=0|access-date=2021-11-28|website=plantillustrations.org}}</ref>

==Description==
[[Image:Pistiabotanical.jpg|left|thumb|19th-century illustration of ''Pistia stratiotes''|340x340px]]
''Pistia stratiotes'' is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[monocotyledon]] with thick, soft leaves that form a rosette.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Schmid|first1=Rudolf|last2=Bown|first2=D.|date=November 2000|title=Aroids: Plants of the Arum Family|journal=Taxon|volume=49|issue=4|page=839|doi=10.2307/1223991|jstor=1223991|bibcode=2000Taxon..49..839S |issn=0040-0262}}</ref> It floats on the surface of the water, its [[roots]] hanging submersed beneath floating leaves. The leaves can measure {{Convert abbreviated|2-15|cm|4=1}} long and are light green, with parallel venations and wavy margins.<ref name=":1" /> The surface of the leaves is covered in short, white hairs which form basket-like structures that can trap air bubbles and increase the plant's buoyancy. The spongy [[Ground tissue#Parenchyma|parenchyma]] with large intercellular spaces in the leaves also aids the plant in floating.<ref>{{Citation|last1=Neuenschwander|first1=Peter|chapter=Pistia stratiotes L. (Araceae)|date=2009|chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/CBO9780511576348A025/type/book_part|title=Biological Control of Tropical Weeds Using Arthropods|pages=332–352|editor-last=Muniappan|editor-first=Rangaswamy|place=Cambridge|publisher=Cambridge University Press|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511576348.017|isbn=978-0-511-57634-8|access-date=2021-12-06|last2=Julien|first2=Mic H.|last3=Center|first3=Ted D.|last4=Hill|first4=Martin P.|editor2-last=Reddy|editor2-first=Gadi V. P.|editor3-last=Raman|editor3-first=Anantanarayanan|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref> 
[[File:Pistia stratiotes Keisotyo.jpeg|left|thumb|210x210px|A close-up view of the flower]]
The [[flower]]s are [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], lack [[Petal|petals]], and are hidden in the middle of the plant amongst the leaves. ''Pistia stratiotes'' has a [[Spadix (botany)|spadix inflorescence]], containing one pistillate flower with one [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] and 2–8 staminate flowers with two [[Stamen|stamens]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=December 2017|title=Pistia stratiotes L.|journal=EPPO Bulletin|language=en|volume=47|issue=3|pages=537–543|doi=10.1111/epp.12429|doi-access=free}}</ref> The pistillate and carpellate flowers are separated by folds in the [[spathe]], where the male flowers are located above the female flowers.<ref name=":4" /> Oval, green [[berries]] with ovoid seeds form after successful fertilization. The plant undergoes [[asexual reproduction]] by propagating through [[Stolon|stolons]], yet evidence of sexual reproduction has also been observed in the ponds of [[Southern Brazil]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Freitas Coelho|first1=Flávia|last2=Deboni|first2=Liene|last3=Santos Lopes|first3=Frederico|date=2014-05-29|title=Density-dependent reproductive and vegetative allocation in the aquatic plant ''Pistia stratiotes'' (Araceae)|journal=Revista de Biología Tropical|volume=53|issue=3–4|pages=369–376|doi=10.15517/rbt.v53i3-4.14599|pmid=17354448|issn=2215-2075|doi-access=free}}</ref>

''Pistia stratiotes'' are found in slow-moving rivers, lakes, and ponds. The species displays optimal growth in the temperature range of {{Convert|22-30|C}}, but can endure extreme temperatures up to {{Convert|35|C}}.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Tamada|first1=Katsuya|last2=Itoh|first2=Kazuyuki|last3=Uchida|first3=Yuko|last4=Higuchi|first4=Shunsuke|last5=Sasayama|first5=Daisuke|last6=Azuma|first6=Tetsushi|date=2014-10-27|title=Relationship between the temperature and the overwintering of water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) at Kowataike, a branch of Yodogawa River, Japan|journal=Weed Biology and Management|volume=15|issue=1|pages=20–26|doi=10.1111/wbm.12061|issn=1444-6162}}</ref> As a result, ''Pistia'' ''stratiotes'' do not grow in colder temperatures, beyond the tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. The species also require slightly acidic water in the [[pH]] range of 6.5–7.2 for optimal growth.<ref name=":2" />

==Invasion==
[[File:Manual removal of water lettuce.jpg|thumb|250px|left|Manual removal of water lettuce (''Pistia stratiotes''), Kolkata, West Bengal, India]]

Water lettuce is among the world's most productive freshwater aquatic plants and is considered an [[invasive species]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Muniappan |first1=Rangaswamy |last2=Reddy |first2=Gadi |last3=Raman |first3=Anantanarayanan |title=Biological Control of Tropical Weeds Using Arthropods |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-511-57634-8 |pages=332–352 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511576348.017 }}</ref> The species can be introduced to new areas by water dispersal, fragmentation, and hitchhiking on marine transportation or fishing equipment.<ref>{{Cite web|author=NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory|title=NOAA National Center for Research on Aquatic Invasive Species (NCRAIS)|url=https://nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/greatlakes/FactSheet.aspx?Species_ID=1099|access-date=2021-12-05|website=nas.er.usgs.gov}}</ref> The invasion of ''Pistia stratiotes'' in the ecosystem can lead to environmental and socio-economic ramifications to the community it serves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=öZkan |first=Korhan |last2=Jeppesen |first2=Erik |last3=Johansson |first3=Liselotte S. |last4=Beklioglu |first4=Meryem |date=February 2010 |title=The response of periphyton and submerged macrophytes to nitrogen and phosphorus loading in shallow warm lakes: a mesocosm experiment |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2427.2009.02297.x |journal=Freshwater Biology |language=en |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=463–475 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2427.2009.02297.x |issn=0046-5070}}</ref> In waters with high nutrient content, particularly those that have been contaminated with human loading of [[sewage]] or fertilizers, water lettuce can exhibit weedy overgrowth. It may also become invasive in hydrologically altered systems such as flood control canals and [[Reservoir|reservoirs]].<ref>Kasulo, V. 2000. The impact of invasive species in African lakes. In: The economics of biological invasions (eds. C. Perrings, M. Williamson and S. Dalmozzone). pp. 183–207. Cheltenham, UK: Edward Elgar.</ref> The severe overgrowth of water lettuce can block gas exchange in the surface water, creating hypoxic conditions and eliminating or disrupting various native marine organisms.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Jinqing|last2=Fu|first2=Guihua|last3=Li|first3=Weiyue|last4=Shi|first4=Ying|last5=Pang|first5=Jicai|last6=Wang|first6=Qiang|last7=Lü|first7=Weiguang|last8=Liu|first8=Change|last9=Liu|first9=Jiansheng|date=January 2018|title=The effects of two free-floating plants (''Eichhornia crassipes'' and ''Pistia stratiotes'') on the burrow morphology and water quality characteristics of pond loach (''Misgurnus anguillicaudatus'') habitat|journal=Aquaculture and Fisheries|volume=3|issue=1|pages=22–29|doi=10.1016/j.aaf.2017.12.001|issn=2468-550X|doi-access=free|bibcode=2018AqFis...3...22W }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Carpenter |first=Stephen R. |last2=Lodge |first2=David M. |date=1986 |title=Effects of submersed macrophytes on ecosystem processes |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0304377086900318 |journal=Aquatic Botany |language=en |volume=26 |pages=341–370 |doi=10.1016/0304-3770(86)90031-8}}</ref> Blocking access to sunlight, large mats of water lettuce can shade native submerged plants and alter communities relying on these native plants as a source of food.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://plants.ifas.ufl.edu/node/328 |title=Water Lettuce (''Pistia stratiotes'') |author=Ramey, Victor |year=2001 |publisher=Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants, University of Florida |access-date=26 April 2010}}</ref> The growth of these mats can also get tangled in boat propellers and create challenges for boaters or recreational fishermen.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Invasive Aquatic Plants|url=https://www.invasivespeciescentre.ca/invasive-species/meet-the-species/invasive-aquatic-plants/|access-date=2021-11-30|website=Invasive Species Centre|language=en-CA}}</ref>

''Pistia stratiotes'' feature in the life cycles of certain insect vectors for [[malaria]] and [[filariasis]].<ref name=":3" /> Mosquitoes of the genus ''[[Mansonia (fly)|Mansonia]]'' can lay their eggs under the leaves of aquatic plants, such as ''Pistia stratiotes.'' Twenty-four hours later, the emerging larvae attach to the plant's roots using its siphon tube for respiration. Within a week, larvae can develop into adult mosquitos, making ''Pistia stratiotes'' a potential breeding ground for vectors of infectious disease.<ref>{{cite book |first=K. |last=Park |title=Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine |location=Jabalpur, India |edition=19th |year=2007|publisher=Banarsidas Bhanot|isbn=}}</ref> The moth ''[[Samea multiplicalis]]'' also uses ''Pistia stratiotes'' as its primary host plant. Eggs are laid among leaves and stems of the host plant and larvae hatch and feed intensively as they develop.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Compensatory responses of ''Samea multiplicalis'' larvae when fed leaves of different fertilization levels of the aquatic weed ''Pistia stratiotes''|journal=Entomologia Experimentalis et Applicata|volume=92|issue=2|pages=205–216|doi = 10.1046/j.1570-7458.1999.00539.x|year = 1999|last1 = Wheeler|first1 = G.S|last2=Halpern|first2=M.D|bibcode=1999EEApp..92..205W |s2cid=84780873}}</ref>

===Control===

# Chemical control: Herbicides have been effective in controlling ''Pistia stratiotes:'' diquat, glyphosate, terbutryn, 2,4-D, among many others.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Datta|first1=Subhendu|last2=Kumar|first2=Ajit|date=2012|title=Diversification of Aquaculture|chapter=Effect of Some Herbicides in Controlling the Floating Aquatic weeds|chapter-url=http://rgdoi.net/10.13140/RG.2.1.4166.8967|language=en|doi=10.13140/RG.2.1.4166.8967|publisher=Narendra Publishing House}}</ref> Yet, the use of herbicides must be critically assessed to prevent negative environmental impacts and possible toxic effects on marine life and human health.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Blackburn|first=Robert D.|date=January 1963|title=Evaluating Herbicides against Aquatic Weeds|journal=Weeds|volume=11|issue=1|pages=21–24|doi=10.2307/4040677|jstor=4040677|issn=0096-719X}}</ref>
# Physical control: ''Pistia stratiotes'' can be controlled with mechanical harvesters that remove the water lettuce from the infested waters and transport it to disposal onshore.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2017|title=Pistia stratiotes L.|journal=EPPO Bulletin|language=en|volume=47|issue=3|pages=537–543|doi=10.1111/epp.12429|issn=1365-2338|doi-access=free}}</ref> Larger infestations can be removed with the aid of hydraulic excavators and tractors. To prevent the re-growth of ''Pistia stratiotes'' colonies, a long-term maintenance program should be implemented.
# Biological control: Two species of [[insect]]s are also being used as a [[biological control]]. Adults and larvae of the [[South America]]n [[weevil]] ''[[Neohydronomous affinis]]'' feed on ''Pistia'' leaves, as do the larvae of the moth ''[[Spodoptera pectinicornis]]'' from [[Thailand]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Harley|first1=K. L. S.|last2=Kassulke|first2=R. C.|last3=Sands|first3=D. P. A.|last4=Day|first4=M. D.|date=September 1990|title=Biological control of water lettuce, Pistia stratiotes [Araceae] by Neohydronomus affinis [Coleoptera: Curculionidae]|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02375260|journal=Entomophaga|language=en|volume=35|issue=3|pages=363–374|doi=10.1007/BF02375260|bibcode=1990BioCo..35..363H |s2cid=15801|issn=0013-8959|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Aphrodyanti|first1=Lyswiana|last2=Rosa|first2=Helda Orbani|last3=Samharinto|first3=Samharinto|date=2017-03-21|title=The potential of Spodoptera pectinicornis in controlling water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) in field|journal=Tropical Wetland Journal|url=http://twj.ulm.ac.id/index.php/twj/article/view/40|volume=3|issue=1|pages=10–16|doi=10.20527/twj.v3i1.40|issn=2654-279X|doi-access=free}}</ref> Both are proving to be useful tools in the management of ''Pistia'' ''stratiotes'' through the experimental recovery of benthic communities with hypoxic conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Coetzee|first1=J. A.|last2=Langa|first2=S. D. F.|last3=Motitsoe|first3=S. N.|last4=Hill|first4=M. P.|date=2020-08-03|title=Biological control of water lettuce, Pistia stratiotes L., facilitates macroinvertebrate biodiversity recovery: a mesocosm study|journal=Hydrobiologia|volume=847|issue=18|pages=3917–3929|doi=10.1007/s10750-020-04369-w|bibcode=2020HyBio.847.3917C |s2cid=220948740|issn=0018-8158}}</ref>
The species is set to be banned in the EU from August 2024 to prevent spreading.<ref>{{Citation |title=Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1203 of 12 July 2022 amending Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1141 to update the list of invasive alien species of Union concern |date=2022-07-12 |url=http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg_impl/2022/1203/oj/eng |access-date=2024-03-02 |language=en}}</ref>

==Range==
The center of origin of ''Pistia stratiotes'' has long been a source of debate.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cilliers|first=Catharina J.|date=1987-10-21|title=First Attempt at and Early Results on the Biological Control of Pistia stratiotes L. in South Africa|url=https://koedoe.co.za/index.php/koedoe/article/view/500|journal=Koedoe|language=en|volume=30|issue=1|pages=35–40|doi=10.4102/koedoe.v30i1.500|issn=2071-0771|doi-access=free}}</ref> Nativity to northern Africa is indicated by [[Egyptian hieroglyphics]] and reports of plants meeting the description of ''Pistia'' by Greek botanists, [[Pedanius Dioscorides|Dioscorides]] and [[Theophrastus]] in the [[Nile]] River.<ref name="Indian Medicinal">{{cite book | doi=10.1007/978-0-387-70638-2_1218 | chapter=Pistia stratiotes Linn. Var. Cuneata Engl | title=Indian Medicinal Plants | date=2007 | last1=Khare | first1=C.P. | page=1 | isbn=978-0-387-70637-5 }}</ref> In addition, the co-evolution of ''Pistia stratiotes'' with various insects native to Brazil and Argentina, such as the [[Neohydronomus|water lettuce weevil]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Biological control|work=LSU AgCenter |date=20 June 2019 |url=https://www.lsuagcenter.com/topics/environment/invasive%20species/water-lettuce/biological-control|publisher=[[Louisiana State University|LSU]] College of Agriculture}}</ref> indicates a long-term native tenure in South America.<ref>{{Cite book|last=D.|first=Center, Ted|title=Insects and other arthropods that feed on aquatic and wetland plants|date=2002|publisher=U.S. Dept. of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service|oclc=54673566}}</ref> Fossil specimens dating back to the late [[Pleistocene]] (~12,000 [[Before Present|BP]]) and early [[Holocene]] (~3,500 BP) period are reported from Florida, indicating a native presence in the southeastern United States.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Evans |first1=J.M. |last2=Jacobson |first2=G.L. |last3=Tanner |first3=B.R. |last4=Grimm |first4=E.C. |date=2024 |title=Seeds of Pistia stratiotes L. (water lettuce) in the paleo-sediments of Lake Annie, Florida |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10933-024-00311-5 |journal=Journal of Paleolimnology |volume=72 |issue= 1|pages=1–13 |doi=10.1007/s10933-024-00311-5 |bibcode=2024JPall..72....1E |issn=1573-0417 |doi-access=|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Recent genetic evidence also suggests that ''Pistia'' is not actually a monotypic genus, as had been long assumed.<ref name=":0" /> Instead, ''Pistia'' appears to be composed of at least three genetically distinct, but morphologically and ecologically similar, species at a global scale.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Madeira |first1=Paul T. |last2=Dray |first2=F. Allen |last3=Tipping |first3=Philip W. |date=2022-08-01 |title=The phytogeography and genetic diversity of the weedy hydrophyte, Pistia stratiotes L. |journal=Biological Invasions |language=en |volume=24 |issue=8 |pages=2613–2634 |doi=10.1007/s10530-022-02798-3 |bibcode=2022BiInv..24.2613M |s2cid=255451313 |issn=1573-1464}}</ref>

===Temperate occurrences===
Though ''Pistia stratiotes'' is intolerant of cold temperatures, it has been recorded growing at least temporarily in temperate areas of North America and Europe.<ref name="POWO" /><ref>{{cite web |last1=Hassler |first1=Michael |title=''Pistia'' |url=https://www.worldplants.de/world-plants-complete-list/complete-plant-list#plantUid-33297 |website=World Plants. Synonymic Checklist and Distribution of the World Flora. Version 18.3 |access-date=17 January 2024 |date=16 January 2024}}</ref> In the United States north of the Gulf of Mexico it has been found growing in Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Kansas, Maryland,
Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Rhode Island, South Carolina,
and Wisconsin. One of these occurrences, in Idaho, survives in an area of a river fed by a hot spring. The rest are thought either to be completely eradicated by cold weather or possibly to survive by seed production.<ref>{{cite web |title=Water Lettuce (''Pistia stratiotes'') Ecological Risk Screening Summary |url=https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/Ecological-Risk-Screening-Summary-Water-Lettuce.pdf |website=U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service |access-date=17 January 2024 |date=30 August 2018}}</ref>

==Fossil record==
''Pistia''-like plants appear in the [[fossil]] record during the [[Late Cretaceous]] epoch in rock [[stratum|strata]] from the western interior of North America. They were first described as †'''''Pistia corrugata''''' by [[Leo Lesquereux]] in 1876 based on specimens from the [[Almond Formation]] of [[Wyoming]] (late [[Campanian]] age). However, based on more complete specimens from the Campanian [[Dinosaur Park Formation]] of southern [[Alberta]], [[Canada]], and other areas, they were redescribed as a separate [[genus]], †'''''Cobbania''''', primarily due to differences in leaf morphology.<ref name=Stockey>{{cite journal|author1=Stockey, R.A.|author2=Rothwell, G.R.|author3=Johnson, K.R.|year= 2007|title=''Cobbania corrugata'' gen. et comb. nov. (Araceae): A floating aquatic monocot from the Upper Cretaceous of western North America|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=94|issue=4|pages= 609–624|doi=10.3732/ajb.94.4.609|pmid=21636430|jstor=27733220 |bibcode=2007AmJB...94..609S }}</ref><ref name=Stockey2>{{cite journal|author1=Stockey, R.A.|author2= Rothwell, G.R.|author3= Johnson, K.R. |year=2016|title= Evaluating relationships among floating aquatic monocots: A new species of ''Cobbania'' (Araceae) from the Upper Maastrichtian of South Dakota|journal=International Journal of Plant Sciences|volume=177|issue =8|pages=706–725|doi=10.1086/688285|bibcode= 2016IJPlS.177..706S|s2cid= 89477112}}</ref> Younger fossils attributed to ''Pistia'' ''stratiotes'' have described from [[Eocene]] strata in the [[southeastern United States]],<ref name="Evans">{{Cite journal|last=Evans|first=Jason M.|date=July 1, 2013|title=Pistia stratiotes L. in the Florida Peninsula: Biogeographic Evidence and Conservation Implications of Native Tenure for an 'Invasive' Aquatic Plant|url=http://www.conservationandsociety.org/article.asp?issn=0972-4923;year=2013;volume=11;issue=3;spage=233;epage=246;aulast=Evans;type=0|journal=Conservation and Society|volume=11|issue=3|page=233|doi=10.4103/0972-4923.121026|via=www.conservationandsociety.org|doi-access=free}}</ref> and 350 [[fossil]] [[seeds]] of †'''''Pistia sibirica''''' have been described from middle Miocene strata of the Fasterholt area near [[Silkeborg]] in [[Central Jutland]], [[Denmark]]. Fossils of this species have also been described from the [[Oligocene]] and Miocene of [[Western Siberia]] and from the Miocene of [[Germany]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Angiosperm Fruits and Seeds from the Middle Miocene of Jutland (Denmark)|author=Else Marie Friis|author-link=Else Marie Friis|publisher=The Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters|volume=24|year= 1985|issue=3 |url=https://www.royalacademy.dk/Publications/Low/369_Friis,%20Else%20Marie.pdf}}</ref>

A specimen of ''Pistia'' from the [[Florida]] peninsula dating from at least 3,550 years [[Before Present]] and a report of [[Holocene]] ''Pistia'' fossils from a lake in south central Florida are consistent with genetic evidence indicating that some varieties of ''Pistia stratiotes'' are native to the southeastern United States.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=Evans /><ref name="Berry">{{cite journal|last1=Berry|first1=E.W.|year=1917|title=The fossil plants from Vero, Florida|journal=The Journal of Geology|volume=25|issue=7|pages=661–666|bibcode=1917JG.....25..661B|doi=10.1086/622533|jstor=30062509|s2cid=128893139}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Consumption===
While considered edible, ''Pistia stratiotes'' is not palatable as it is rich in [[calcium oxalate]] crystals that are bitter in taste. Nevertheless, there are records of the plant being utilized as famine food in India during the [[Great Famine of 1876–1878]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Les|first=Donald H.|chapter=Monocotyledons I|date=2020 |title=Aquatic Monocotyledons of North America|pages=3–214|publisher=CRC Press|doi=10.1201/9781315166339-2|doi-broken-date=12 July 2025 |isbn=978-1-315-16633-9|s2cid=243190762}}</ref>

The [[Hausa people|Hausa]] people of Nigeria used the ash of the plant as a substitute for salt due to its high concentration of [[potassium chloride]], a mineral salt.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Gupta|first1=R|last2=Tripathi|first2=P|last3=Kumar|first3=R|last4=Sharma|first4=AK|last5=Mishra|first5=A|date=2010|title=Pistia stratiotes (Jalkumbhi)|journal=Pharmacognosy Reviews|volume=4|issue=8|pages=153–160|doi=10.4103/0973-7847.70909|pmid=22228955|pmc=3249915|issn=0973-7847|doi-access=free}}</ref> This salt substitute, also called ''zakankau'', was of high importance, especially when imported salt was unavailable.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Hygrophila auriculata in Global Plants on JSTOR|url=https://plants.jstor.org/compilation/hygrophila.auriculata|access-date=2021-12-06|website=plants.jstor.org}}</ref>

[[File:20210623 Hortus botanicus Leiden - Pistia stratiotes v1.jpg|thumb|''[[Heteranthera reniformis]]'' with ''Pistia stratiotes'']]

Caution is advised when consuming ''Pistia stratiotes'', as the plant is a [[hyperaccumulator]], and can absorb and accumulate toxic heavy metals present in its environment.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lu|first1=Qin|last2=He|first2=Zhenli L.|last3=Graetz|first3=Donald A.|last4=Stoffella|first4=Peter J.|last5=Yang|first5=Xiaoe|date=July 2011|title=Uptake and distribution of metals by water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes L.)|journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research International|volume=18|issue=6|pages=978–986|doi=10.1007/s11356-011-0453-0|issn=1614-7499|pmid=21287283|bibcode=2011ESPR...18..978L |s2cid=30818232}}</ref> The presence of high concentrations of calcium oxalate crystals can induce various health concerns, such as inhibited mineral absorption and kidney stones.<ref>{{Cite web|date=19 March 2012|title=Water Lettuce|url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/water-lettuce/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kumar|first1=Parveen|last2=Patel|first2=Mikita|last3=Oster|first3=Robert A.|last4=Yarlagadda|first4=Vidhush|last5=Ambrosetti|first5=Adam|last6=Assimos|first6=Dean G.|last7=Mitchell|first7=Tanecia|date=2021|title=Dietary Oxalate Loading Impacts Monocyte Metabolism and Inflammatory Signaling in Humans|journal=Frontiers in Immunology|volume=12|page=105|article-number=617508 |doi=10.3389/fimmu.2021.617508|pmid=33732242|pmc=7959803|issn=1664-3224|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In Singapore and Southern China, ''Pistia stratiotes'' is commonly grown or collected as animal feed for ducks and pigs.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Handbook of Utilization of Aquatic Plants|url=https://www.fao.org/3/x6862e/X6862E08.htm|access-date=2021-11-30|website=www.fao.org}}</ref> Water lettuce is also considered an alternative for poultry feed in Indonesia due to its high content of crude protein.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Use of Pistia stratiotes in diets of Kampong chicken|url=http://www.lrrd.org/lrrd32/7/agus32113.html|access-date=2021-11-30|website=www.lrrd.org}}</ref>

=== Medical treatment ===
There are various medical uses of ''Pistia stratiotes'' throughout regions in Asia and Africa. In Nigeria, the dried leaves are prepared into a powder form and are applied to wounds and sores [[Disinfectant|for disinfection]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ajibesin|first=Kola' Kayode|date=2012-11-25|title=Ethnobotanical Survey of Plants Used for Skin Diseases and Related Ailments in Akwa Ibom State, Nigeria|url=https://ethnobotanyjournal.org/index.php/era/article/view/588|journal=Ethnobotany Research and Applications|language=en|volume=10|pages=463–522|issn=1547-3465}}</ref> A similar use is present in [[Ayurveda|Indian traditional medicine]], where the powdered leaf is applied to [[syphilitic]] eruptions and [[skin infections]].<ref name="Shyamsundar 2005 127">{{Cite journal|last1=Shyamsundar|first1=D|last2=Premkumar|first2=VG|date=2005|title=Antidermatophytic activity of Pistia stratiotes|journal=Indian Journal of Pharmacology|volume=37|issue=2|page=127|doi=10.4103/0253-7613.15116|issn=0253-7613|doi-access=free}}</ref> In [[Nigeria]] and [[Gambia]], the leaf is infused in water to create an [[eyewash]] to treat [[allergic conjunctivitis]].<ref name="Koffuor 2014 274">{{Cite journal|last1=Koffuor|first1=George Asumeng|last2=Kyei|first2=Samuel|last3=Asiamah|first3=Emmanuel A|last4=Atobiga|first4=Clement Nsobire|last5=Awuah|first5=Agnes|last6=Abokyi|first6=Samuel|date=2014|title=Antiallergic effect of an aqueous leaf extract of Pistia stratiotes in murine model of ovalbumin-induced allergic conjunctivitis|journal=Pharmacognosy Research|volume=6|issue=4|pages=274–279|doi=10.4103/0974-8490.138243|pmid=25276062|pmc=4166813|issn=0974-8490 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The eyewash is known to have a cooling and [[analgesic]] effect. Therefore, the plant is commonly called 'eye-pity' in Africa.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pistia stratiotes Linn. [family ARACEAE] on JSTOR|url=https://plants.jstor.org/stable/10.5555/al.ap.upwta.1_447|access-date=2021-11-29|website=plants.jstor.org}}</ref> In addition, the leaves of ''Pistia stratiotes'' can be burned into [[ash]], and in Indian and Nigerian traditional medicine, the ash is used in treating [[Dermatophytosis|ringworm]] infections of the [[scalp]].<ref name="Shyamsundar 2005 127"/>

==== Medicinal properties ====

* Anti-inflammatory properties: Extractions of the leaves of ''P. stratiotes'' reduces mast infiltration and degranulation in allergic reactions and presents [[anti-inflammatory]] properties.<ref name="Koffuor 2014 274"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Koffuor|first1=G. A.|last2=Kyei|first2=S.|last3=Woode|first3=E.|last4=Ekuadzi|first4=E.|last5=Ben|first5=I. O.|date=2012|title=Possible mechanism of anti-inflammatory activity and safety profile of aqueous and ethanolic leaf extracts of Pistia stratiotes Linn (Araceae)|url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/jgsa/article/view/84194|journal=Journal of the Ghana Science Association|language=en|volume=14|issue=1|pages=69–81|issn=0855-3823}}</ref> The ethanolic extracts have also been positively correlated with a reduction in inflammatory disorders, such as [[arthritis]] and [[fever]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Koffuor|first1=George|last2=Kyei|last3=Boampong|date=March 2012|title=Antiarthritic effect of aqueous and ethanolic leaf extracts of Pistia stratiotes in adjuvant-induced arthritis in Sprague-Dawley rats|journal=Journal of Experimental Pharmacology|volume=4|pages=41–51|doi=10.2147/jep.s29792|pmid=27186115|pmc=4863544|issn=1179-1454 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
*Antifungal properties: With the popular use of ''Pistia stratiotes'' as a traditional treatment for ringworms, researchers have tested ''P. stratiotes'' methanolic extracts on [[dermatophyte]] fungi. The results of the studies depicted significant [[Fungicide|fungicidal]] activity on ''[[Trichophyton rubrum|T. rubrum]]'', ''T. mentagrophytes'', and ''[[Epidermophyton floccosum|E. floccosum]]''.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Gupta|first1=Arti|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W380EAAAQBAJ&dq=fungi+pistia+ringworm&pg=PA43|title=Fungal Diseases in Animals: From Infections to Prevention|last2=Singh|first2=Nagendra Pratap|date=2021|publisher=Springer Nature|isbn=978-3-030-69507-1|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Shyamsundar 2005 127"/>

=== Environmental remediation ===
The high sorption property of water lettuce makes it a great candidate for biodegradable oil sorbents in marine oil spills. Particularly, the leaves of ''Pistia'' ''stratiotes'' can efficiently absorb significant amounts of hydrocarbons due to its large surface area and hydrophobicity.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gaballah|first1=M. S.|last2=Ismail|first2=K.|last3=Beltagy|first3=A.|last4=Zein Eldin|first4=A. M.|last5=Ismail|first5=M. M.|date=May 2019|title=Wastewater Treatment Potential of Water Lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) with Modified Engineering Design|journal=Journal of Water Chemistry and Technology|volume=41|issue=3|pages=197–205|doi=10.3103/s1063455x1903010x|bibcode=2019JWCT...41..197G |s2cid=197402470|issn=1063-455X}}</ref>

As a hyper-accumulator, ''Pistia'' ''stratiotes'' has been studied as a potential candidate for [[wastewater treatment]] plants. The roots and leaves of the plant have been found to absorb excess nutrients and heavy metals, such as [[zinc]], [[chromium]], and [[cadmium]] in contaminated waters.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rodrigues|first1=Ana Carolina Dornelas|last2=do Amaral Sobrinho|first2=Nelson Moura Brasil|last3=dos Santos|first3=Fabiana Soares|last4=dos Santos|first4=André Marques|last5=Pereira|first5=Ana Carolina Callegario|last6=Lima|first6=Erica Souto Abreu|date=2017-03-28|title=Biosorption of Toxic Metals by Water Lettuce (Pistia stratiotes) Biomass|journal=Water, Air, & Soil Pollution|volume=228|issue=4|page=156|doi=10.1007/s11270-017-3340-6|bibcode=2017WASP..228..156R|s2cid=100580905|issn=0049-6979}}</ref><ref name=":5" /> ''Pistira stratiotes'' has also been shown to accumulate mercury in its roots.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Rezania |first=Shahabaldin |last2=Taib |first2=Shazwin Mat |last3=Md Din |first3=Mohd Fadhil |last4=Dahalan |first4=Farrah Aini |last5=Kamyab |first5=Hesam |date=2016 |title=Comprehensive review on phytotechnology: Heavy metals removal by diverse aquatic plants species from wastewater |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhazmat.2016.07.053 |journal=Journal of Hazardous Materials |volume=318 |pages=587–599 |doi=10.1016/j.jhazmat.2016.07.053 |issn=0304-3894|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

''Pistia'' ''stratiotes'' can be grown in water gardens to reduce [[harmful algal bloom]]s and eutrophic conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ali |first=Esmat F. |last2=Galal |first2=Tarek M. |last3=Hassan |first3=Loutfy M. |last4=Al-Yasi |first4=Hatim M. |last5=Dakhil |first5=Mohammed A. |last6=Eid |first6=Ebrahem M. |date=2021-01-01 |title=Seasonal potential of Pistia stratiotes in nutrient removal to eliminate eutrophication in Al-Sero Drain (South Nile Delta, Egypt) |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02705060.2021.1915397 |journal=Journal of Freshwater Ecology |language=en |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=173–187 |doi=10.1080/02705060.2021.1915397 |issn=0270-5060|doi-access=free }}</ref> The plant is able to control the growth of algae by restricting light penetration in the water column and competing for nutrients, with significant uptake of [[phosphorus]] and [[ammonia]] nitrogen.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Xiang|last2=Wu|first2=Hao|last3=Chen|first3=Junren|last4=Ye|first4=Jinyun|date=2013-05-08|title=Effects of allelochemical extracted from water lettuce (Pistia stratiotes Linn.) on the growth, microcystin production and release of Microcystis aeruginosa|journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research|volume=20|issue=11|pages=8192–8201|doi=10.1007/s11356-013-1783-x|pmid=23653319|bibcode=2013ESPR...20.8192W |s2cid=103835|issn=0944-1344}}</ref>
